title: Advancing zero-shot and multilingual generalization in large language models

items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have recently gained prominence as intelligent software tools and areused in most phases of the software development life cycle (SDLC). While source code generation hasbeen widely studied, the generation of performant source code has received very little research attention. Although automatic code parallelization tools exist in the non-LLM setting, their analogue in the context of transformation using pre-trained models requires investigation. In this work, we perform a comparative study of 23 pre-trained LLMs considering the state-of-the-art Intel C Compiler (icc) as the baseline auto-parallelization tool. Our motivation is to investigate how well LLMs play the role of an auto-parallelizer, given a sequential C source code. Our experiments show that, in some instances, LLM-based zero-shot source code parallelization outperforms icc in non-functional aspects, such as speedup. Using 30 kernels from the popular PolyBench C benchmarks, we evaluated 23 pre-trained LLMs, generating 667 parallelized code versions. We identified notable performance gains after filtering out those with compilation errors or data race issues through comprehensive memory and threading error analysis. Across all tested LLMs, 26.66% of cases achieved a speedup surpassing that of the state-of-the-art (icc). The best-performing LLM-generated code achieved a parallelization speedup of 7.5× compared to the icc-parallelized version (speedup of 1.08×). Our study shows that pre-trained LLMs tasked with zero shot sequential to parallel code translation, i.e., even without fine-tuning or chain-of-thought prompting (or feedback prompts), perform competitively with non-LLM based compiler technology that has been developed over the past decades.

items.abstract: <jats:p>Rapid detection of active wildfires from satellite imagery is critical for emergency response and resource allocation. Traditional operational systems rely on thermal anomaly algorithms applied to sensors such as VIIRS and MODIS, which excel at global monitoring but can miss small or obscured fires under smoke and cloud cover. Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) offer flexible, instruction-following image understanding that could complement thermal-based detection through visual screening of satellite scenes. This study evaluates three leading VLMs, Gemini 2.5 Flash, LlaVA, and Llama 3.2-Vision, for binary active-fire classification. We used a simple yes/no prompt across each image of a 500 image satellite imagery dataset. Our results indicate mean accuracies of 0.98 for Gemini 2.5 Flash, 0.728 for LlaVA, and 0.966 for Llama 3.2-Vision. Gemini 2.5 Flash had significant evidence and 95% confidence to prove its feasiblity for this application. The findings demonstrate feasibility of VLM-based fire screening but highlight some small limitations including reliance on visible-spectrum imagery without thermal bands, absence of temporal context, and lack of domain adaptation to satellite radiometry. Future work should incorporate multispectral inputs, temporal reasoning, and rigorous benchmarking against operational fire products to assess practical utility of these VLMs in satellite fire detection applications.</jats:p>

items.abstract: <jats:p>Rapid detection of active wildfires from satellite imagery is critical for emergency response and resource allocation. Traditional operational systems rely on thermal anomaly algorithms applied to sensors such as VIIRS and MODIS, which excel at global monitoring but can miss small or obscured fires under smoke and cloud cover. Recent advances in vision-language models (VLMs) offer flexible, instruction-following image understanding that could complement thermal-based detection through visual screening of RGB satellite scenes. This study evaluates three open and closed source VLMs, Gemini 2.5 Flash, LlaVA, and Llama 3.2-Vision, for binary active-fire classification using a simple yes/no prompt across three independent trials of eight randomly sampled images each from a 500image dataset. Results indicate mean accuracies of 0.98 for Gemini 2.5 Flash, 0.728 for LlaVA, and 0.966 for Llama 3.2-Vision. Gemini 2.5 Flash had significant evidence and 95% confidence to prove its feasiblity for this application. The findings demonstrate feasibility of VLM-based fire screening but highlight some small limitations including reliance on visible-spectrum imagery without thermal bands, absence of temporal context, and lack of domain adaptation to satellite radiometry. Future work should incorporate multispectral inputs, temporal reasoning, and rigorous benchmarking against operational fire products to assess practical utility of these VLMs in satellite fire detection applications.</jats:p>
